questions.title: Does Minn. Stat. § 181.101 authorize employees to recover "average daily wage penalties," or are such penalties enforceable only by the Commissioner?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the interaction between MPWA §§ 181.171 and 181.101. Section 181.171 says an employer who violates certain MPWA sections is liable for "compensatory damages and other appropriate relief," and also for "the civil penalties or damages provided for in the section violated." Cohen argued § 181.101's plain language lets employees obtain average daily wage penalties, but the panel held only the Commissioner can collect penalties under § 181.101(a) after serving a demand for payment. How does the court reconcile § 181.171's broad remedial language with § 181.101's Commissioner-centric penalty mechanism? Is the key that § 181.101 "provides for" civil penalties only for the Commissioner, whereas other MPWA sections (like §§ 181.13 and 181.14) expressly grant employees penalty rights? If so, is "other appropriate relief" under § 181.171 limited to non-penalty relief unless the violated section expressly authorizes private penalties?

questions.title: Can a private MFLSA plaintiff seek statutory penalties that are payable only to the Commissioner, and does Laidlaw provide Article III standing in that scenario?
questions.question_body: The opinion says the parties agree MFLSA statutory penalties (unlike wages and liquidated damages) are payable to the Commissioner, not Cohen. The court remands to determine jurisdiction, citing Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw for the idea that civil penalties can deter and thus redress ongoing harms. But the concurrence questions whether Laidlaw fits the MFLSA context. Is there a Minnesota-law basis for a private plaintiff to ask a federal court to impose MFLSA penalties that are then paid to the Commissioner? If yes, does Laidlaw's deterrence rationale supply Article III redressability when the plaintiff doesn't receive the penalties? What differences between Laidlaw's citizen-suit environmental penalties and MFLSA penalties might defeat standing here (e.g., statutory design, who may sue, state vs. federal enforcement scheme)?

questions.title: What must Consilio show on remand to establish mootness via voluntary cessation of its overtime policy, and who bears the burden?
questions.question_body: The panel vacates and remands the MFLSA penalty issue because the record is unclear whether Consilio's allegedly unlawful overtime policy is still in place. If the policy is gone and won't recur, the claim may be moot; if not, Laidlaw suggests penalties could still deter. On remand, what evidence must Consilio present to make it "absolutely clear" the challenged conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur? Does Consilio bear a "heavy burden" under the voluntary cessation doctrine? Practically, would declarations of a permanent policy change suffice, or does the court look for written rescission, compliance audits, or other objective indicia? And does the fact that wages and liquidated damages were paid already affect the mootness analysis for penalties?

questions.title: Is there a private right or remedy for MWTA notice violations under § 181.032, and did Cohen waive any such claim on appeal?
questions.question_body: Cohen alleged Consilio failed to provide the written notice of a change in overtime policy required by the Minnesota Wage Theft Act (MWTA), Minn. Stat. § 181.032(f), (d)(4), and sought penalties. The court affirmed dismissal, noting Cohen stipulated he received all pay due and pointed to no statutory authority allowing civil penalties under § 181.032, and further found he offered no meaningful appellate argument (citing waiver). Does § 181.032 create any private cause of action or remedy for notice failures independent of unpaid wages (e.g., statutory penalties, injunctive relief)? If remedies exist, are they enforceable only by the Commissioner, or can employees sue directly? Finally, was the court's waiver holding based on inadequate briefing alone, or also on the absence of a statutory penalty provision in § 181.032?

questions.title: Did Cohen forfeit his request for injunctive relief by changing it at summary judgment, and could the court have treated it as a Rule 15 amendment?
questions.question_body: Cohen's complaint sought certain injunctive relief, but at summary judgment he pivoted and asked for an order requiring Consilio to rescind its 2019 overtime policy. The panel says the district court "understandably" didn't consider this new request because new claims must be raised by amended complaint (citing InfoDeli and Rule 15(a)). Could the court have construed Cohen's briefing as an implicit motion to amend, or used Rule 15(b)'s "amendment to conform to the evidence"? Does Rule 15(b) even apply at summary judgment (as opposed to trial)? If Cohen amends on remand to seek rescission specifically, does that help with standing/mootness, or would any injunctive request still be moot if the policy is already rescinded?

questions.title: Should the district court have resolved Article III standing/mootness before granting summary judgment, and does the parties’ stipulation affect that sequencing?
questions.question_body: The parties stipulated to a procedure where the court would decide summary judgment on the MPWA, MFLSA, and MWTA claims, acknowledging a full grant would end the case. The panel ultimately vacates the MFLSA ruling for a jurisdiction check. Under Steel Co.'s prohibition on hypothetical jurisdiction, should the district court have addressed standing/mootness on the MFLSA penalties issue before reaching the merits? Can a parties’ stipulation about an "expedient path" ever justify deciding the merits first, or must the court always confirm Article III jurisdiction sua sponte? If jurisdiction was uncertain only as to one claim, was it proper to reach the merits of the other claims while remanding the jurisdictional question for the MFLSA claim?

questions.title: What is the effect on putative class claims when the named plaintiff receives full wages and liquidated damages before class certification?
questions.question_body: Cohen filed on behalf of a putative class, but then stipulated he was paid all overtime wages and MFLSA liquidated damages he sought. The opinion focuses on his individual claims and does not discuss class certification status. In the Eighth Circuit, if a named plaintiff's individual monetary claims are satisfied before class certification, are putative Rule 23 class claims mooted (distinguishing Genesis Healthcare and Campbell-Ewald)? Does it matter that penalties (if any) would go to the Commissioner rather than the plaintiff? Are there any anti-"pick off" doctrines applicable under Minnesota wage statutes that would preserve a live class controversy despite full payment to the named plaintiff?

questions.title: What is the posture of attorney’s fees, costs, and prejudgment interest after the panel’s partial vacatur, given the concurrence’s note?
questions.question_body: Judge Kobes's concurrence says he "also vacate[s] the district court’s ruling as to attorney’s fees, costs, and prejudgment interest," but the majority opinion doesn't expressly address fees, costs, or prejudgment interest. What is the operative effect—are those collateral issues automatically reopened because the MFLSA ruling was vacated, or only to the extent they depend on the MFLSA claim? In wage cases under Minnesota law, can a plaintiff recover attorney’s fees or prejudgment interest independent of obtaining penalties (e.g., based solely on recovered wages/liquidated damages already paid pre-judgment), and does the timing of payment affect entitlement?
